case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a student seeking damages under Title II of the ADA and Section 504 for a public school’s failure to provide appropriate disability-related educational services must prove “bad faith or gross misjudgment,” or instead may proceed under the ordinary ADA/Section 504 discrimination standards (with deliberate indifference as the usual mens rea for compensatory damages).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. §§ 12131–12134 (especially § 12132), and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 794 (and related remedies provisions, including 42 U.S.C. § 12133 and 29 U.S.C. § 794a).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Eighth Circuit improperly heightened the burden for ADA/Section 504 claims in the K–12 education/IDEA-services context by requiring proof of “bad faith or gross misjudgment,” a judge-made standard that appears nowhere in the statutory text, conflicts with how Title II and Section 504 are interpreted in other contexts, and undermines the statutes’ anti-discrimination purposes. Petitioner (supported by the United States and amici) contends that courts should apply the ordinary elements of an ADA/Section 504 claim—i.e., denial of benefits/meaningful access or failure to reasonably accommodate by reason of disability—and that when compensatory damages are sought the proper culpability standard is the familiar ‘deliberate indifference’ framework rather than a more demanding “bad faith or gross misjudgment” requirement that effectively immunizes schools for serious failures tied to disability-related needs.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that this case sits at the intersection of two “distinct but complementary” statutory schemes: IDEA (ensuring a free appropriate public education through specialized procedures and educational judgments) and the ADA/Rehabilitation Act (anti-discrimination). In that overlap, respondents contend, ordinary ADA/Section 504 standards cannot simply be transposed onto disputes about the adequacy of IDEA services without transforming routine educational-program disagreements into federal damages actions. They therefore defend the Eighth Circuit’s use of a heightened “bad faith or gross misjudgment” requirement in this specific context as a necessary doctrinal boundary that respects deference to educational expertise, prevents ADA/Section 504 from becoming an end-run around IDEA’s framework, and distinguishes discrimination from mere alleged misjudgments in special-education programming.
key_precedents: Cleveland v. Policy Mgmt. Sys. Corp., 526 U.S. 795 (1999)
Timms v. Metro. Sch. Dist. (1st Cir.)
B.R. ex rel. Rempson v. District of Columbia, 524 F. Supp. 2d 35 (D.D.C. 2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press the federalism/IDEA-overlap concern and the need for an administrable boundary separating discrimination from mere disputes over educational methodology. But Barnes’s Spending Clause notice logic does not authorize us to invent an education-specific “bad faith or gross misjudgment” element untethered from Title II and §504’s text; if anything, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, Barnes points toward uniform remedial limits already familiar from Title VI/Title IX—i.e., compensatory damages only for intentional discrimination, commonly satisfied by deliberate indifference. The discrimination/adequacy line can be policed through existing statutory elements—“by reason of/solely by reason of” causation and meaningful-access/reasonable-accommodation requirements—plus IDEA exhaustion where applicable, without rewriting the mens rea for one sector. A narrow holding rejecting only the Eighth Circuit’s categorical heightened scienter rule best preserves institutional legitimacy while leaving lower courts room to dismiss routine FAPE-adequacy claims that do not plausibly allege disability-based denial of access.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that the text of Title II and § 504 does not spell out “bad faith or gross misjudgment,” and their reliance on Barnes v. Gorman properly centers the Spending Clause notice principle. But Barnes’s notice logic still requires a clear, administrable line between actionable discrimination (“by reason of”/“solely by reason of”) and mere disputes over the adequacy of individualized educational programming—an area IDEA specifically channels through procedures and deference to pedagogical judgment. Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s proposal to use Gebser/Davis “deliberate indifference” does not resolve that line-drawing problem in this context, because “knowledge + unreasonable response” risks turning contested methodological choices into damages exposure whenever a court later deems the choice inadequate. Absent a textual command to convert IDEA-adjacent service-delivery disagreements into compensatory-damages litigation under Title II/§ 504, I would retain the Eighth Circuit’s limiting standard as the best available proxy for the statutes’ discrimination requirement and affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Title II and §504 do not expressly say “bad faith or gross misjudgment,” and I take seriously their point that Barnes v. Gorman favors administrable, familiar remedial limits. But Barnes’s Spending Clause notice logic still supports a tighter boundary in this IDEA-adjacent context, because recipients would not clearly understand that ordinary disputes about individualized educational programming choices—often contestable and method-dependent—expose them to compensatory damages on a “deliberate indifference” theory that risks collapsing into after-the-fact disagreement about reasonableness. The deliberate-indifference model from Gebser/Davis, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, was crafted for known misconduct (harassment) and does not map neatly onto pedagogical judgments where “knowledge” of a child’s needs is ubiquitous and the real dispute is adequacy; without a heightened screen, ADA/§504 threatens to become an end-run around IDEA’s structured remedial scheme. I therefore would affirm a limiting standard (whether framed as bad faith/gross misjudgment or an equivalently stringent intent requirement) to preserve the discrimination/adequacy line the statutory text presupposes (“by reason of” disability) and to avoid a damages regime Congress did not clearly authorize here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press the IDEA-overlap and Spending Clause notice concern: we should not turn ADA/§504 into routine damages litigation over pedagogical disagreements. But their proposed “bad faith or gross misjudgment” screen is untethered to the text and functions too much like near-immunity in precisely the context where disabled children depend on public systems; it risks insulating known failures to accommodate as long as officials can label them “professional judgment.” As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, Barnes’s cross-referenced remedial framework points to the familiar Title VI/Title IX intent requirement, and deliberate indifference supplies an administrable, non-negligence boundary that preserves notice while still providing redress for knowing denial of meaningful access. The discrimination/adequacy line can be policed through exhaustion (where applicable) and the statutes’ existing elements—causation “by reason of,” reasonable accommodation, and meaningful access—without importing an education-specific mens rea that Congress did not enact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press the IDEA-overlap and federalism worry: we should not let ADA/§504 damages become routine second-guessing of pedagogical judgments. But that policy concern cannot justify adopting Monahan’s “bad faith or gross misjudgment” gloss, which is untethered from the text of §12132 and §794(a) and sits awkwardly with the remedial cross-references that, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh note, point us to Barnes and the familiar Title VI/Title IX deliberate-indifference framework for compensatory damages. The notice/Spending Clause rationale does not support a context-specific, judge-made mens rea; it supports uniform, administrable limits already embedded in the incorporated remedial scheme, while the discrimination/adequacy line can be policed through causation (“by reason of/solely by reason of”), meaningful-access/reasonable-accommodation principles, and (where applicable) IDEA exhaustion rather than rewriting the statute. Deliberate indifference is not perfect, but it is a known, workable threshold that screens out negligence and ordinary disputes without creating near-immunity in the very setting where access rights matter most.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s federalism/Spending Clause notice concern is the hardest point: we should not let ADA/§504 become a general damages regime for ordinary disagreements over educational methodology. But under a textualist approach that policy anxiety cannot justify adding a school-specific “bad faith or gross misjudgment” element absent from § 12132 and § 794(a), especially when Barnes points us to the Title VI/Title IX remedial analogue rather than to context-specific judicial carveouts. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Gebser/Davis supply an already demanding, administrable intent limit—deliberate indifference—for compensatory damages, while the discrimination/adequacy boundary can be enforced through the statutes’ own elements (“by reason of,” reasonable accommodation/meaningful access) and IDEA’s separate exhaustion structure. I therefore see no lawful basis to affirm an atextual heightened mens rea rule simply to manage overlap with IDEA.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s best point is the federalism/IDEA-overlap worry that ADA/§504 damages could invite courts to second-guess pedagogical judgments, and they invoke Spending Clause notice to justify a “bad faith or gross misjudgment” screen. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Barnes’s notice logic cuts toward applying the familiar, uniform Title VI/Title IX remedial framework Congress incorporated—an intent requirement satisfied by Gebser/Davis deliberate indifference—rather than creating an education-specific, atextual mens rea that risks near-immunity. Deliberate indifference, combined with the statutes’ existing discrimination elements (“by reason of/solely by reason of,” meaningful access/reasonable accommodation, and causation) and IDEA exhaustion where applicable, supplies an administrable limiting principle without rewriting the enacted scheme. Thomas’s concern that deliberate indifference could collapse into hindsight merits scrutiny, but under our precedents it still requires knowledge of a substantial risk and a conscious failure to act, which is meaningfully more than negligence or methodological disagreement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that IDEA’s domain and federalism concerns require a heightened “bad faith or gross misjudgment” screen to keep ADA/§504 from becoming a damages forum for pedagogical disagreements—identifies a real boundary problem, but it proposes an atextual solution. Under a textualist/originalist approach, the limiting principles must come from the enacted elements (“by reason of”/“solely by reason of” causation, meaningful access/reasonable accommodation) and from the remedial cross-references; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Barnes’s Spending Clause notice logic points toward the familiar Title VI/Title IX intent requirement (deliberate indifference for compensatory damages), not an education-specific scienter gloss. The “gross misjudgment” test lacks statutory footing, risks variable application across contexts, and effectively rewrites generally applicable antidiscrimination statutes to protect a particular sector. IDEA overlap can be managed through exhaustion where applicable and careful application of causation and deliberate-indifference thresholds, without adding a judge-made near-immunity rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—Spending Clause notice and the need to keep ADA/§504 from becoming a damages backdoor for IDEA/FAPE adequacy fights—is real, but it does not justify the Eighth Circuit’s atextual “bad faith or gross misjudgment” overlay. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Barnes’s notice logic points toward the familiar Title VI/Title IX remedial analogue, where compensatory damages require intentional discrimination shown through deliberate indifference, not a context-specific near-immunity rule. Deliberate indifference meaningfully addresses their administrability concern by excluding negligence and routine methodological disagreement while still providing redress when officials know of a substantial risk that a student is being denied meaningful access and nonetheless fail to act. IDEA overlap can be policed through exhaustion where applicable and through the existing statutory elements (causation and reasonable accommodation), rather than rewriting the mens rea standard in a way that predictably undermines procedural fairness for students with disabilities.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title II and Section 504 prohibit exclusion or denial of benefits “by reason of” disability, and their remedial provisions incorporate the ordinary discrimination framework rather than atextual heightened intent tests. Nothing in 42 U.S.C. §§ 12132–12133 or 29 U.S.C. §§ 794, 794a supports requiring “bad faith or gross misjudgment” as an element for damages in the K–12 services setting; that standard traces to Monahan and policy concerns about IDEA overlap, not statutory text. Consistent with Barnes v. Gorman’s treatment of Title II/§504 remedies by analogy to Spending Clause statutes, compensatory damages turn on an intent standard commonly articulated as deliberate indifference, which supplies a narrower, administrable limit without insulating serious failures. A narrow holding can preserve IDEA’s procedures (including exhaustion where required) while rejecting the Eighth Circuit’s categorical heightened mens rea as inconsistent with the statutes and our remedial precedents.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Neither Title II’s operative text (“by reason of” disability, 42 U.S.C. § 12132) nor § 504’s text (“solely by reason of,” 29 U.S.C. § 794(a)) creates a freestanding federal damages remedy for disputes over the adequacy of educational programming; in the K–12 FAPE context, courts must police the line between discrimination and second-guessing pedagogical judgments that Congress primarily channeled through IDEA. Because Title II borrows § 504’s remedies (42 U.S.C. § 12133; 29 U.S.C. § 794a), and this Court has treated such remedial schemes as limited by notice and consent principles (Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002)), it is permissible to require a heightened showing before imposing compensatory damages on state and local school systems for educational-service decisions. The Eighth Circuit’s “bad faith or gross misjudgment” rule functions as a boundary ensuring that damages attach only to truly discriminatory or conscience-shocking departures, rather than mere negligence or disagreement over special-education methodology. Given federalism concerns and the absence of any clear textual command to convert IDEA-type adequacy disputes into ordinary ADA/§ 504 damages actions, I would affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Neither 42 U.S.C. § 12132 nor 29 U.S.C. § 794(a) speaks to how courts should police alleged deficiencies in individualized special-education programming, and importing ordinary ADA/§504 discrimination standards into that domain risks converting routine IDEA service disputes into federal damages actions with substantial practical consequences for school administration. Consistent with Spending Clause notice principles reflected in Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181, 185–89 (2002), and the deliberate-indifference framework drawn from Title IX cases like Gebser, damages should be reserved for culpable misconduct rather than mere educational misjudgments. A “bad faith or gross misjudgment” screen is a sensible limiting principle in this overlapping IDEA context to preserve deference to educational judgment and avoid using ADA/§504 as an end-run around IDEA’s remedial scheme. Nothing in the statutes’ remedial cross-references (42 U.S.C. § 12133; 29 U.S.C. § 794a) clearly authorizes damages liability for ordinary disputes over adequacy of services absent such heightened culpability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Nothing in Title II’s text, 42 U.S.C. § 12132, or Section 504, 29 U.S.C. § 794, imposes a “bad faith or gross misjudgment” element, and importing that judge-made hurdle would unduly narrow the broad remedial scheme Congress adopted for disability discrimination in public services, including public schools. Under this Court’s damages framework for Spending Clause antidiscrimination statutes, remedies for Title II/§504 track Title VI/Title IX principles; as Barnes v. Gorman explains, those statutes supply the baseline for the scope of implied private remedies, and the usual requirement for compensatory damages is intentional discrimination shown by deliberate indifference, not a heightened education-specific carveout. A “gross misjudgment” rule risks insulating serious failures to provide reasonable accommodations or meaningful access—harms that fall most heavily on children with disabilities and their families—from effective redress. The better approach is to apply ordinary ADA/§504 discrimination standards, with deliberate indifference serving as the mens rea for compensatory damages, preserving IDEA’s process without creating near-immunity where schools deny disability-related access to education.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Nothing in Title II’s operative text—“no qualified individual with a disability shall, by reason of such disability, be excluded” from a public entity’s services, programs, or activities, 42 U.S.C. § 12132—or in Section 504’s parallel prohibition, 29 U.S.C. § 794(a), creates a school-specific liability overlay requiring “bad faith or gross misjudgment.” The remedies provisions likewise point the other way: Title II incorporates § 504 remedies via 42 U.S.C. § 12133, and § 504 incorporates Title VI’s remedial framework via 29 U.S.C. § 794a(a)(2), which under Barnes v. Gorman supports importing familiar Title VI-style limits, including deliberate indifference as the mens rea typically required for compensatory damages, rather than a heightened, judge-made standard. While IDEA’s structure counsels against converting ordinary educational disputes into damages suits, that boundary can be enforced through existing ADA/§ 504 elements (e.g., meaningful access/reasonable accommodation and causation “by reason of” disability) and the deliberate-indifference requirement for damages, without adding an atextual “gross misjudgment” rule. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools reinforces that ADA/§ 504 and IDEA are distinct schemes, and it does not authorize rewriting ADA/§ 504 standards in the K–12 context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The operative text of Title II and § 504 prohibits disability-based exclusion or denial of benefits by any public entity or federally funded program, and it contains no carveout requiring a plaintiff in the K–12/IDEA-services setting to prove “bad faith or gross misjudgment.” See 42 U.S.C. § 12132; 29 U.S.C. § 794(a). For compensatory damages, our cases looking to Title VI/Title IX remedial principles under these statutes point to an “intent” requirement satisfied by deliberate indifference, not by extra-statutory hurdles invented for one context. See Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181, 185–89 (2002); Gebser v. Lago Vista Indep. Sch. Dist., 524 U.S. 274, 287–90 (1998). Respect for IDEA’s distinct procedures may limit what counts as discrimination and may bear on exhaustion or merits in a given case, but separation-of-powers and textualist principles do not permit courts to rewrite the ADA/§ 504 standard by adding a heightened mens rea nowhere enacted by Congress.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Neither Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132, enforced via § 12133) nor Section 504 (29 U.S.C. § 794, with remedies via § 794a) contains a “bad faith or gross misjudgment” prerequisite, and we should be cautious about grafting an extra-statutory, context-specific hurdle onto generally applicable anti-discrimination statutes absent a clear historical or textual basis. For compensatory damages, the Court’s Spending Clause notice cases indicate the proper intent requirement is deliberate indifference—an “exacting” standard that already prevents liability for mere negligence or programmatic disagreements while preserving workable boundaries for schools. Gebser v. Lago Vista Indep. Sch. Dist. and Davis v. Monroe County Bd. of Educ. supply that deliberate-indifference framework, and it has been carried over in the lower courts to Title II/§ 504 damages claims to ensure recipients have fair notice of when monetary liability attaches. Retaining deliberate indifference (rather than “bad faith or gross misjudgment”) better fits precedent, is more administrable, and avoids undermining uniform interpretation of Title II and Section 504 across settings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Title II and §504 broadly prohibits exclusion or denial of benefits “by reason of” disability, without carving out a special education-services exception or imposing a heightened scienter requirement like “bad faith or gross misjudgment.” See 42 U.S.C. § 12132; 29 U.S.C. § 794(a). For damages, our remedial cases instruct courts to look to the incorporated Title VI/Title IX framework, under which deliberate indifference suffices to show the requisite intent for compensatory relief. See 42 U.S.C. § 12133; 29 U.S.C. § 794a; Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181, 185–89 (2002); Gebser v. Lago Vista Indep. Sch. Dist., 524 U.S. 274, 290 (1998). Whatever boundary-drawing is appropriate to prevent ADA/§504 from becoming a generalized appeal of IDEA adequacy determinations must come from the statutes’ elements and established remedial limits, not acontextual, judge-made “gross misjudgment” gloss absent from the enacted text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title II and Section 504 prohibit disability discrimination in categorical terms—"no qualified individual" shall be excluded or denied benefits "by reason of" disability, 42 U.S.C. § 12132; 29 U.S.C. § 794(a)—and nothing in that text authorizes a special, heightened "bad faith or gross misjudgment" carveout for K–12 educational-services disputes. Consistent with this Court’s remedial framework treating ADA/§504 damages as coextensive with Title VI/Title IX analogs, Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181, 185–89 (2002), the usual intent requirement for compensatory damages is satisfied by deliberate indifference rather than a judge-made standard that risks insulating serious, known failures to accommodate. Deliberate indifference also respects practical consequences by preventing liability for mere negligence while ensuring procedural fairness and meaningful access for students with disabilities. Importing a heightened mens rea absent statutory grounding would undermine the statutes’ equal-protection-like promise of equal access and invite inconsistent standards across contexts governed by the same operative provisions.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a student seeking damages under Title II of the ADA and Section 504 for disability-based denial of equal access to education services must prove “bad faith or gross misjudgment” by school officials (as the Eighth Circuit requires), or instead must satisfy the same discrimination standard that applies outside the IDEA/FAPE context.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. §§ 12131–12134, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 794 (and their enforcement/damages standards as applied in K–12 public education).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Eighth Circuit’s heightened “bad faith or gross misjudgment” requirement improperly adds an extra element to ADA/Section 504 liability in the school-education setting, lacks any grounding in the statutory text, and conflicts with the Supreme Court’s instruction that identical statutory language should not be given different meanings depending on context. Petitioner (supported by the United States and amici) contends that ADA/Section 504 claims concerning access to educational programs/services should be evaluated under the ordinary discrimination framework applicable in other contexts (with the appropriate mens rea only as required for the particular remedy, e.g., damages), rather than a special, education-only immunity-like standard derived from overlap with the IDEA.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that this case sits at the intersection of the IDEA (which governs the adequacy of special-education services through the FAPE/IEP process) and the ADA/Section 504 (which prohibit discrimination). In that overlap, they contend, courts properly apply a heightened standard—requiring proof of “bad faith or gross misjudgment”—to prevent ADA/Section 504 from becoming an alternative vehicle for routine disputes about the content or implementation of IDEA services. Respondents emphasize that this is a distinct, “conceptually peculiar” context where mistakes in educational judgment should not be recast as disability discrimination absent extraordinary culpability.
key_precedents: Cleveland v. Policy Mgmt. Sys. Corp., 526 U.S. 795 (1999)
Timms v. Metro. Sch. Dist., 722 F.2d (1st Cir.)
B.R. ex rel. Rempson v. District of Columbia, 524 F. Supp. 2d 35 (D.D.C. 2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press the administrability concern that ADA/§504 damages not become an end-run around IDEA disputes and routine pedagogical judgments, but his proposed cure—an education-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” overlay—lacks a textual foothold and risks creating a near-immunity inconsistent with the statutes’ general terms. As Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Barnes v. Gorman points us to the Title VI/IX remedial framework, which supplies a narrower and more legitimate limiting principle: compensatory damages require intentional discrimination, commonly shown by deliberate indifference, rather than a heightened culpability standard unique to schools. Justice Thomas’s uniform-meaning point (invoking Clark v. Martinez) reinforces the institutional cost of assigning different operative meanings to the same language merely because the setting is K–12. A minimalist disposition can reject the Eighth Circuit’s categorical rule while underscoring that ordinary disagreements over IEP/FAPE adequacy, without more, do not establish disability discrimination or intentionality for damages.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that an unqualified damages regime could invite litigants to repackage IDEA/FAPE disputes as ADA/§504 claims, but that administrability concern cannot justify adding an education-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” element absent any textual footing. As the Chief Justice explains, Barnes v. Gorman directs attention to the remedial limitation—compensatory damages generally require intentional discrimination (often deliberate indifference)—which addresses notice and overdeterrence without rewriting the liability standard embedded in “by reason of” and “solely by reason of.” Alito’s effort to treat “gross misjudgment” as a proxy for intent is not what the statutes say, and it conflicts with the uniform-meaning principle reflected in Clark v. Martinez that identical operative language should not silently narrow in the K–12 context. The IDEA can do the education-specific work Congress assigned to it, including exhaustion and FAPE-specific procedures, without judicially conferring near-immunity on schools under Title II and §504.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts is right that the text lacks an education-specific carveout, but the strongest countervailing point is that Barnes v. Gorman and the Title VI/IX remedial analogy already treat damages as turning on a culpability screen, and in the K–12 FAPE/IEP context “bad faith or gross misjudgment” functions as a practical proxy for the sort of intentional discrimination that warrants compensatory damages without federalizing routine pedagogical disputes. Justice Thomas’s Clark v. Martinez uniform-meaning concern has some pull, yet I do not read our approach as changing what it means to be excluded “by reason of” disability; rather, it identifies the heightened showing needed before imposing money damages where the alleged wrong is intertwined with educational discretion and IDEA’s comprehensive scheme. Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh propose “deliberate indifference” as the narrower limiting principle, but Gebser/Davis arose in settings with clearer notice and more discrete prohibited conduct; importing that standard here risks making damages liability turn on hindsight disagreements about complex, individualized educational judgments. Given those practical consequences and the need to preserve IDEA’s primacy while still allowing recovery for truly egregious conduct, I remain persuaded the Eighth Circuit’s rule is a defensible, administrable constraint in this specialized context.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is administrability: the fear that ADA/§504 damages will swallow IDEA and invite federal courts to referee everyday pedagogical disputes. But that concern is addressed by the remedial intent requirement our colleagues (Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan) emphasize from Barnes v. Gorman’s Title VI/IX framework—compensatory damages already require “intentional discrimination,” commonly deliberate indifference, which screens out negligence without inventing an education-only near-immunity rule untethered to statutory text. Alito’s effort to treat “bad faith or gross misjudgment” as a proxy for intent still improperly raises the culpability bar above the established Barnes/Gebser/Davis structure and predictably closes courthouse doors to students who are effectively excluded from educational benefits. Consistent with Justice Barrett’s Clark v. Martinez point, identical antidiscrimination language should not be narrowed only for K–12; IDEA overlap can be managed through exhaustion and by distinguishing access/exclusion from mere FAPE-adequacy disagreements.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that, in the K–12 IEP/FAPE setting, a deliberate-indifference standard might invite damages litigation that second-guesses pedagogical judgment and functions as an IDEA end-run. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Barnes v. Gorman and our Title VI/IX remedial framework already provide a textually coherent screen—compensatory damages require intentional discrimination (often deliberate indifference)—without rewriting liability by importing an education-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” rule. Justice Barrett’s Clark v. Martinez point matters here: once we graft a special culpability overlay onto identical operative language, we undermine statutory coherence and create context-specific near-immunities untethered to the text. Workability concerns can be handled through remedies and existing IDEA-exhaustion and claim-framing doctrines (distinguishing access discrimination from mere IEP adequacy disputes), rather than narrowing the substantive prohibition “by reason of” disability.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the strongest point for the respondent, but his proposed cure—importing a K–12-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” screen—lacks any textual anchor in Title II’s or §504’s prohibition on exclusion “by reason of” disability, and it conflicts with the uniform-meaning impulse Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas identify (cf. Clark v. Martinez). Even accepting Alito’s premise that routine pedagogical disputes pose line-drawing problems, our precedents already address that at the remedial stage: as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain, Barnes v. Gorman’s Title VI/IX framework cabins compensatory damages to intentional discrimination (commonly deliberate indifference), avoiding negligence-based liability without rewriting the elements of a statutory violation. Alito’s effort to treat “gross misjudgment” as a proxy for intent effectively elevates culpability beyond what Barnes and the Gebser/Davis line require and risks creating an education-only near-immunity Congress did not enact. IDEA overlap can be managed through exhaustion and by insisting that ADA/§504 claims target discriminatory denial of access/benefits rather than mere disagreement about FAPE adequacy, which preserves separation-of-powers by leaving policy adjustments to Congress.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—the administrability risk that ADA/§504 damages could become an IDEA end-run—deserves respect, but it cannot justify importing an education-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” element that has no textual footing in §12132 or §794(a). As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Barnes v. Gorman’s Title VI borrowing already supplies the proper, precedent-based limiter at the remedial stage: compensatory damages require intentional discrimination (commonly shown by deliberate indifference), which protects notice and screens out mere negligence without creating a K–12 near-immunity. Justice Thomas’s Clark v. Martinez uniform-meaning point further underscores the institutional costs of giving identical statutory prohibitions a narrower meaning in schools absent congressional direction. The IDEA’s domain can be protected through existing tools—exhaustion and careful separation of access/exclusion claims from pure FAPE-adequacy disputes—rather than rewriting ADA/§504 liability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the strongest point on the other side, but under an originalist/textualist approach it cannot justify grafting an education-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” element onto Title II/§504’s context-neutral prohibitions, which speak in terms of exclusion or denial of benefits “by reason of” disability. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Barnes v. Gorman’s Title VI analogy—together with Gebser/Davis—already supplies the proper limiting principle at the remedial stage: compensatory damages require intentional discrimination (often deliberate indifference), which screens out negligence and many ordinary pedagogical disputes without rewriting liability. Justice Alito’s attempt to treat “bad faith or gross misjudgment” as a proxy for intent still effectively elevates culpability beyond what our remedial precedents require, and it risks violating the uniform-meaning principle reflected in Clark v. Martinez by narrowing identical statutory language only in the K–12 setting. The IDEA’s domain is protected through exhaustion and by insisting that FAPE/IEP disagreements, without more, do not establish discrimination—rather than by inventing a quasi-immunity standard untethered to the enacted text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is administrability—avoiding conversion of routine IEP/FAPE disputes into ADA/§504 damages litigation—but I do not see a legitimate interpretive path to his education-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” overlay. As the Chief Justice explains, Barnes v. Gorman’s Title VI/IX remedial framework already supplies the necessary screen: compensatory damages require “intentional discrimination,” typically satisfied by deliberate indifference, which addresses notice and overdeterrence without rewriting liability. Alito’s claim that “bad faith or gross misjudgment” is merely a proxy for intent still functionally narrows the operative statutory prohibition in one context, running into the uniform-meaning concern Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan identify (cf. Clark v. Martinez) and risking under-protection where disability-based exclusion is real but not easily labeled “gross.” The IDEA’s exhaustion and procedural architecture can do the work of channeling pedagogical disagreements, leaving ADA/§504 to address genuine access/benefits denial with the ordinary intent-for-damages constraint.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title II and Section 504 use broadly applicable, context-neutral prohibitions on discrimination—42 U.S.C. § 12132 and 29 U.S.C. § 794(a)—and nothing in that text supports an education-only “bad faith or gross misjudgment” overlay that effectively narrows the statutes in one setting but not others. Our Spending Clause damages cases require intentional discrimination as a condition for monetary liability, and that intent is satisfied by deliberate indifference, not a higher culpability threshold; Gebser v. Lago Vista and Davis v. Monroe County set that baseline, and Barnes v. Gorman confirms looking to that Title IX/Title VI remedial framework for ADA/§504 damages. A narrow ruling can preserve the IDEA’s role by distinguishing mere disputes over FAPE/IEP adequacy from claims alleging denial of equal access, while rejecting the Eighth Circuit’s categorical heightened standard as inconsistent with the uniform meaning of the operative statutory language. This approach respects precedent and institutional legitimacy by aligning education cases with the settled deliberate-indifference intent requirement for damages rather than creating a circuit-specific immunity-like rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title II and § 504 prohibit disability-based exclusion and denial of benefits by their terms, 42 U.S.C. § 12132 and 29 U.S.C. § 794(a), and nothing in that text creates an education-specific element requiring proof of “bad faith or gross misjudgment.” Importing such a heightened standard from the IDEA/FAPE context effectively amends the statutes and departs from textualism; where Congress wanted special rules for education disputes, it provided them in the IDEA, not by altering ADA/§ 504 liability. Clark v. Martinez instructs that identical statutory language should not be given different meanings depending on context, which cuts against an education-only gloss on discrimination. To the extent intent is relevant for damages, Barnes v. Gorman limits remedies consistent with the statutes’ structure (including Spending Clause analogies for § 504), but it does not authorize courts to add an extra liability element untethered to the text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title II and §504 do not expressly supply a free-standing damages standard for K–12 educational service disputes that overlap with the IDEA’s FAPE/IEP regime, and it is sensible to require more than ordinary error in educational judgment before labeling such disputes “disability discrimination.” Given that compensatory damages under Title II/§504 already require intentional discrimination (commonly satisfied by “deliberate indifference”), see Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002), the Eighth Circuit’s “bad faith or gross misjudgment” rule functions as a practical limiting principle preventing ADA/§504 from becoming an end-run around the IDEA’s specialized procedures and standards. The petitioner’s reliance on uniform-meaning cases like Clark v. Martinez, 543 U.S. 371 (2005), is less persuasive here because the question concerns the culpability threshold for damages in a “conceptually peculiar” educational context where courts should hesitate to constitutionalize—or federalize via discrimination law—routine pedagogical disagreements. As a matter of practical consequences and administrability, the heightened standard appropriately protects school officials’ discretionary judgments and avoids exposing districts to expansive damages liability absent extraordinary culpability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title II of the ADA and § 504 contain no education-specific carveout, so the Eighth Circuit’s “bad faith or gross misjudgment” requirement improperly adds an extra element of liability untethered to statutory text. This Court has repeatedly cautioned that identical statutory language should not be given different meanings depending on context, and nothing in the ADA or § 504 supports a special immunity-like threshold for K–12 schools. The proper way to address concerns about overdeterring educational judgment is through the remedial mens rea for damages—most courts require “intentional discrimination” shown by deliberate indifference, consistent with this Court’s damages framework under Spending Clause analogs rather than an education-only heightened standard. Requiring “bad faith or gross misjudgment” would unjustifiably narrow access to judicial relief for vulnerable students facing real-world exclusion from public educational services in violation of 42 U.S.C. §§ 12131–12134 and 29 U.S.C. § 794.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The operative text of Title II and Section 504 establishes a single, generally applicable prohibition—no qualified individual shall, “by reason of” disability, be excluded from participation in or denied benefits, 42 U.S.C. § 12132; 29 U.S.C. § 794(a)—and it contains no education-specific “bad faith or gross misjudgment” overlay. Under our interpretive principle that identical statutory language should not be given different meanings depending on context, Clark v. Martinez counsels against importing an extra element solely for K–12 education. For damages, Barnes v. Gorman confirms that Title II/§504 remedies track the Title VI model, under which compensatory damages turn on an intent standard (commonly deliberate indifference), leaving no textual or remedial basis to ratchet that up to an education-only near-immunity. Workability concerns about IDEA/FAPE disputes are better handled through existing doctrinal lines (e.g., exhaustion and differentiating access discrimination from adequacy-of-services claims), not by rewriting the discrimination standard.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The operative statutory text contains no education-specific carveout: Title II commands that “no qualified individual with a disability shall, by reason of such disability,” be denied benefits of a public entity’s services, 42 U.S.C. § 12132, and § 504 likewise forbids exclusion “solely by reason of” disability, 29 U.S.C. § 794(a). The Eighth Circuit’s “bad faith or gross misjudgment” requirement adds an extra-textual element applicable only in one context, contrary to the principle that identical language should receive a consistent meaning across applications absent textual warrant. Concerns about converting IDEA/FAPE disputes into damages actions can be handled through existing remedial mens rea limits—most notably the deliberate-indifference standard tied to clear-notice principles for damages recognized in Title VI/IX analogs and applied to § 504/Title II remedies. Under Barnes v. Gorman, courts look to the Title VI/IX remedial framework for these statutes, which supports limiting damages via intent standards rather than creating a special, immunity-like liability rule for education cases.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title II and §504 expressly borrow Title VI’s remedial scheme, and under this Court’s precedents compensatory damages generally require “intentional discrimination” (commonly satisfied by deliberate indifference), not an education-only overlay of “bad faith or gross misjudgment.” See Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002). The Eighth Circuit’s heightened standard lacks grounding in the statutory text and risks giving identical language different meanings depending on context, contrary to our interpretive approach. Practical workability and institutional concerns can be addressed through existing doctrines (e.g., deliberate-indifference intent for damages and IDEA exhaustion rules), rather than by creating a special liability barrier for K–12 students seeking equal access under the ADA/§504.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Neither Title II nor Section 504 contains any education-specific culpability requirement, and nothing in their texts authorizes courts to impose a heightened “bad faith or gross misjudgment” element as a condition of liability or damages in the K–12 setting. Consistent with Clark v. Martinez, identical statutory language should not be given different meanings depending on context; importing Monahan’s overlay risks creating a school-only immunity not rooted in the statutes’ original public meaning. For compensatory damages, our remedial precedents treat Title II/§504 as Title VI analogues, and Barnes v. Gorman confirms that the available remedies track those for Spending Clause antidiscrimination statutes—supporting an “intentional discrimination” requirement (often satisfied by deliberate indifference), not an idiosyncratic “gross misjudgment” test. Precedent and methodological consistency therefore favor applying the ordinary ADA/§504 discrimination framework (with the appropriate intent showing for damages) rather than a special standard derived from IDEA/FAPE overlap.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title II and Section 504 forbid disability discrimination in broad, evenhanded terms, and neither statute’s text creates an education-only carveout requiring proof of “bad faith or gross misjudgment” to establish a violation. Under this Court’s consistency principle, identical statutory language should not be given different meanings depending on context, and importing a heightened culpability threshold here conflicts with that approach. The proper place to account for culpability is at the remedial stage: as Barnes v. Gorman explains, Section 504 and Title II borrow Title VI’s remedial framework, under which compensatory damages generally require “intentional discrimination” (often satisfied by deliberate indifference), not an extra, immunity-like “gross misjudgment” overlay. Procedural safeguards in the IDEA can manage FAPE/IEP disputes without distorting ADA/Section 504’s discrimination standard or denying children an equal-access remedy when schools effectively exclude them from educational benefits on the basis of disability.
